Decision support — the clinician decides.

Edit & re-run

At a glance

Robotic repair has not been shown to improve pain, complications, recurrence or quality of life over laparoscopic repair; it costs more and usually takes longer (low certainty).

Pain coughing at 24 hmedian NRS 4 with rTAPP vs 5 with TEP, P=0.431 [3]
Complications (pooled RCTs)RR 0.76 (95% CI 0.49-1.17), robotic vs laparoscopic [9]
Median cost$3258 with robotic vs $1421 with laparoscopic TAPP, P<.001 [1]
Operative time75.5 min with robotic vs 40.5 min with laparoscopic (median), P<.001 [1]

Main caveat: a few small trials with experienced surgeons and short follow-up, underpowered for recurrence and chronic pain; one open-label trial (ROLAIS) found fewer complications with robotic repair [4].

Bottom line
Certainty: Low

Randomised trials show no consistent benefit of robotic over laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair for pain, complications, recurrence, quality of life or return to activity, while robotic repair costs more per case and usually takes longer [1, 2, 3, 6, 9]. The one trial favouring robotic repair (ROLAIS/DIRECT, fewer complications and shorter time) was open-label and single-centre [4, 5]. The trials are underpowered for recurrence and chronic pain, so equivalence on these outcomes cannot be claimed [9].

Few small, mostly single-centre trials with short follow-up; inconsistent operative-time results; imprecise for rare outcomes.

What this means for clinical practice

Default choice

Laparoscopic (TAPP or TEP) repair; robotic repair offers no proven patient benefit and costs more [1, 3, 9].

Who may benefit

The evidence does not identify any patient group; benefits in obese patients and in recurrent or complex hernias are untested in RCTs, and the only trial favouring robotic repair involved highly experienced robotic surgeons [4, 5].

Counselling

Expect similar pain, recovery, complication and recurrence risk with either approach; robotic surgery usually takes longer and costs more, and long-term data are limited [2, 3, 6].

Cost per case

Robotic repair costs roughly USD 595not traced more (Switzerland, rTAPP $3327 vs TEP $2732) to USD 1837not traced more (US, robotic $3258 vs laparoscopic TAPP $1421) per case [1, 3]; the Italian public-payer model gives an incremental cost of €2,224 [12]; Indian costs are not known.

Postoperative and chronic painRCTs and meta-analyses6 numbersThere was no difference in early or late pain.Low

Evidence: ROGER, Indian AIIMS RCT, RIVAL (2020 and 2023 reports of one trial), meta-analysis of RCTs

There was no difference in early or late pain. In ROGER, median NRS pain while coughing at 24 h was 4 with rTAPP vs 5 with TEP (P=0.431) [3]. In the Indian RCT, VAS mean differences (robotic minus laparoscopic) were 0.28 (95% CI -0.34 to 0.90) at 3 h, -0.16 (-0.69 to 0.37) at 6 h and 0.32 (-0.15 to 0.79) at 12 h [6]. Rescue analgesia was needed by 20.6% with robotic vs 17.9% with laparoscopic repair [6]. RIVAL found similar pain at 30 days, 1 year and 2 years [1, 2]. For chronic pain, the pooled RR was 0.53 (95% CI 0.20-1.39) from 2 RCTs [9].

Postoperative complicationsRCTs and meta-analyses6 numbersPooled RCTs show no significant difference in complications (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.49-1.17).Low

Evidence: ROGER, ROLAIS, RIVAL, stray-energy RCT; RCT meta-analyses (overlapping pools)

Pooled RCTs show no significant difference in complications (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.49-1.17) [9]. Other RCT meta-analyses agree: RR 0.89 (0.45-1.78) [10] and RR 0.83 (0.34-2.03) [15]. In ROGER, complications occurred in 9 patients (10%) with rTAPP vs 10 (11%) with TEP [3]. In ROLAIS, open-label, complications were 23.0% with R-TAPP vs 41.5% with L-TAPP, and haematomas 6.8% vs 18.5% [4]. Port-site thermal injury occurred in 60% of robotic vs 49% of laparoscopic samples (p=0.548) [8].

Evidence: RIVAL 2-year follow-up, ROLAIS; observational-dominated meta-analysis

In RIVAL at 2 years there was 1 recurrence with robotic vs 1 with laparoscopic repair (P=1.0) [2]. ROLAIS and ROGER found no difference [3, 4]. A mostly observational meta-analysis reported RR 0.32 (95% CI 0.17-0.59) favouring robotic repair; this is non-randomised and not causal [11].

Operative timeRCTs and meta-analyses6 numbersRobotic repair was longer in three trials: median 75.5 min with robotic vs 40.5 min with laparoscopic TAPP; 80.3 min with rTAPP vs 64.2 min with TEP; 64.9 min with robotic vs 31.7 min with laparoscopic.Low

Evidence: RIVAL, ROGER, VOLTAIRE, ROLAIS/DIRECT (one trial), Indian AIIMS RCT; RCT meta-analyses

Robotic repair was longer in three trials: median 75.5 min with robotic vs 40.5 min with laparoscopic TAPP [1]; 80.3 min with rTAPP vs 64.2 min with TEP [3]; 64.9 min with robotic vs 31.7 min with laparoscopic [7]. It was shorter in ROLAIS (-13.4 min) [4] and its DIRECT analysis (simple hernias 51 vs 60 min, robotic vs laparoscopic) [5]. The Indian RCT found no difference (p=0.142) [6]. Pooled RCTs give MD +18.5 min (95% CI -8.4 to 45.5; I2 97.7%) [10] and MD +17.6 min (-20.7 to 55.9; I2 98.8%) [15].

Costmixed evidence5 numbersMedian cost was $3258 with robotic vs $1421 with laparoscopic TAPP.Moderate

Evidence: RIVAL, ROGER; Italian model-based cost-utility analysis

Median cost was $3258 with robotic vs $1421 with laparoscopic TAPP [1]. Mean unilateral procedural cost was $3327 with rTAPP vs $2732 with TEP [3]. An Italian model estimated an incremental cost of €2,224 for 0.05 QALYs gained, an ICER of €44,480/QALY, with under 25% probability of cost-effectiveness at €30,000/QALY [12]. This model is not trial-based and ignores robot acquisition and learning-curve effects.

Evidence: ROLAIS only; observational meta-analysis

In ROLAIS, same-day discharge was 95.9% with R-TAPP vs 81.5% with L-TAPP (P=0.012) [4]. Mostly observational data show no significant difference in length of stay (MD +0.33 days, 95% CI -0.03 to 0.70) [11].

Pooled RCT estimates for specific complications showed no significant difference for r-TAPP vs l-TAPP: seroma RR 0.40 (95% CI 0.08-2.03), haematoma RR 0.65 (0.12-3.41) and surgical site infection RR 0.33 (0.03-3.14) [10]. Readmission RR was 0.71 (0.09-5.58) in the short-term RCT pool [15]. [10, 14, 15]

Why Low: Sparse events, wide CIs, overlapping small RCT pools

Details

Conflicting evidence5ROLAIS (with its DIRECT secondary analysis, one trial) found fewer complications (23.0% robotic vs 41.5% laparoscopic) and shorter operating time with robotic TAPP. RIVAL and ROGER found no complication difference and longer robotic operating time. The difference may reflect ROLAIS's open-label…
  • ROLAIS (with its DIRECT secondary analysis, one trial) found fewer complications (23.0% robotic vs 41.5% laparoscopic) and shorter operating time with robotic TAPP [4, 5]. RIVAL and ROGER found no complication difference and longer robotic operating time [1, 3]. The difference may reflect ROLAIS's open-label design, its CRP primary outcome, its unusually high laparoscopic complication rate, unbalanced withdrawals, and very experienced robotic surgeons (at least 100 r-TAPP each) [4, 5].
  • A mostly observational meta-analysis (17 of 18 cohorts observational) reported lower recurrence with robotic repair (RR 0.32, 95% CI 0.17-0.59) [11]. The RCTs show no difference, with only 1 recurrence per arm at 2 years in RIVAL [2, 9]. The observational signal is prone to confounding and is not causal.
  • A meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis found lower pain with robotic TAPP than laparoscopic TEP (MD -1.59, 95% CI -2.41 to -0.76) [13]. Its pool appears to include non-randomised studies, and the finding comes from sensitivity analysis. It conflicts with the blinded ROGER RCT, which compared the same approaches and found no pain difference [3].
  • VOLTAIRE found more robotic patients back to normal activity at 14 days [7, 9]. The blinded Indian RCT found no difference in time to resumption of activities (p=0.180) [6]. VOLTAIRE was small, unequally allocated, used an open-console robot and had ergonomics as its focus [7].
  • Pooled operative-time estimates range from no difference (MD 0.59 min) to clearly longer robotic surgery (MD +30.04 min), with I2 around 98% [10, 11, 14, 15]. The spread is driven by trial design and surgeon experience. The largest pooled estimate (+30.04 min) is mostly observational [11].
Applicability3The randomised evidence covers mostly elective, uncomplicated, primary unilateral (some bilateral) inguinal hernias in predominantly male adults, operated on by experienced minimally invasive surgeons. ROGER excluded recurrent hernias. The Indian trial enrolled uncomplicated hernias only. There are…
Case mix
The randomised evidence covers mostly elective, uncomplicated, primary unilateral (some bilateral) inguinal hernias in predominantly male adults, operated on by experienced minimally invasive surgeons [1, 3, 4, 6]. ROGER excluded recurrent hernias [3]. The Indian trial enrolled uncomplicated hernias only [6]. There are no dedicated randomised data for obese patients, recurrent or bilateral hernias, or the robotic learning curve [9]. Most trials compared robotic TAPP with laparoscopic TAPP, but ROGER's comparator was laparoscopic TEP and VOLTAIRE used an open-console robot [3, 7].
India and cost
One blinded single-centre RCT from AIIMS, India found no difference in early pain, rescue analgesia, operative time or return to activity [6]. That trial reported no cost data. All cost figures come from the US, Switzerland and an Italian model, all showing higher robotic cost per case [1, 3, 12]. Indian per-case costs, robot acquisition and maintenance costs, and the cost-effectiveness of robotic repair in Indian hospitals are not known from this evidence. The modelled analyses do not capture robot acquisition or learning-curve effects.
Training
The Italian model suggests confining r-TAPP to training programmes [12]. Surgeon workload findings are mixed: frustration was higher with robotic repair in RIVAL [1], while NASA-TLX workload was lower with rTAPP than TEP in ROGER [3] and ergonomic risk was lower in VOLTAIRE [7]. No RCT has assessed the robotic learning curve. ROGER's authors acknowledge that some rTAPP surgeons may not have completed it [3].
What would change this answer4A large multicentre blinded RCT powered for chronic pain and recurrence with at least 2-3 years of follow-up. An independent trial replicating the ROLAIS complication and operative-time advantage with experienced robotic surgeons. RCTs in obese patients and in recurrent or bilateral hernias, and…
  • A large multicentre blinded RCT powered for chronic pain and recurrence with at least 2-3 years of follow-up.
  • An independent trial replicating the ROLAIS complication and operative-time advantage with experienced robotic surgeons.
  • RCTs in obese patients and in recurrent or bilateral hernias, and studies of the robotic learning curve.
  • Trial-based cost-effectiveness analyses including robot acquisition and maintenance costs, especially from India or similar health systems.
Challenged by the skeptic7 caveatsThe conclusion holds with caveats. Randomized evidence is small and low to very low certainty, with about 100-180 patients per trial, experienced surgeons and mostly uncomplicated hernias in men. Verdict: the conclusion holds with caveats.

Caveats
  • Randomized evidence is small and low to very low certainty, with about 100-180not verified patients per trial, experienced surgeons and mostly uncomplicated hernias in men. Equivalence cannot be claimed for rare outcomes such as recurrence or chronic pain.
  • RIVAL was an underpowered pilot with no primary outcome and 25% loss to follow-up at 2 years. RIVAL 2020 and 2023 are the same patients.
  • ROLAIS and DIRECT are the same trial and are not independent. ROLAIS reported fewer complications and shorter operative time but was single-centre and open-label.
  • Comparators are heterogeneous: ROGER compared robotic TAPP with laparoscopic TEP, VOLTAIRE used an open-console robot, and the Indian RCT used 2:1 allocation.
  • Operative time results are inconsistent across trials (robotic longer in RIVAL, VOLTAIRE and ROGER, shorter in ROLAIS) with I2 around 98%.
  • Cost evidence is a model-based Italian cost-utility analysis (ICER €44,480/QALY) plus RIVAL cost data ($3258 vs $1421); no RCT-based cost-effectiveness analysis exists, and it ignores robot acquisition and learning-curve effects.
  • The lower-recurrence signal comes from observational data and should not be treated as causal. No guideline addressing robotic vs laparoscopic inguinal repair was found. No RCT data exist on obesity, recurrent or bilateral hernias, or the learning curve.
Not independent
  • RIVAL 2020 and its 1-2 year follow-up report the same 102 patients. [1] [2]
  • DIRECT is a secondary analysis of the ROLAIS trial (138 vs 139 patients), so they are a single trial. [4] [5]
  • The meta-analyses pool the same small set of RCTs and are not independent confirmations. [9] [10] [14] [15] [13]
Picked for extraction (second wave)
  • Robotic TAPP vs laparoscopic TEP meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis; its pain-benefit claim conflicts with the RCTs and its pool composition needs checking. [13]
  • GRADE-assessed RCT-only meta-analysis of r-TAPP vs l-TAPP; the operative-time result depends on removing one study. [14]
  • RCT-only meta-analysis on short-term outcomes; useful for checking trial overlap and the consistency of the pooled operative time. [15]
What the meta-analyses pooled
  • Pooled 18 cohorts and 78,940 participants, mostly observational; the recurrence RR 0.32 is non-randomised. [11]
  • The pool of 6 studies for r-TAPP vs laparoscopic TEP appears to include non-randomised studies, since the abstract recommends further randomized trials. [13]
  • Counts 7 RCTs reported in 9 publications, so the pool includes secondary reports and overlapping trials such as RIVAL follow-up and ROLAIS/DIRECT; the pool also mixes TAPP and TEP comparators. [9]
  • Pools only 3 RCTs; the operative-time advantage emerges only after removing the heterogeneity-driving study (I2 98%). [14]
Evidence against
  • Single-centre open-label RCT found robotic TAPP gave fewer complications, shorter operating time and more same-day discharge, which conflicts with a 'no difference' conclusion
    “R-TAPP was associated with a shorter operating time (-13.4 min, P < 0.001), fewer complications (23.0% versus 41.5%, P = 0.029), including fewer haematomas (6.8% versus 18.5%, P = 0.043), and a higher same-day discharge rate (95.9% versus 81.5%, P = 0.012).”
    [4]
  • Pooled mostly non-randomised data show lower recurrence with robotic repair
    “robotic repair was associated with a lower observed recurrence risk (RR 0.32, 95% CI 0.17-0.59; I2 = 0%), although certainty was low and the randomized evidence was imprecise.”
    [11]
  • Trial sequential analysis suggests lower postoperative pain with robotic TAPP versus laparoscopic TEP
    “Sensitivity and trial sequential analyses suggested a significant reduction in postoperative pain with R-TAPP, with TSA confirming robust evidence for lower pain scores”
    [13]

Other notable findings from this run7The extractor could not match 10 numbers to the papers' wording; they are kept and labelled “not verified” in the trials table. DIRECT, labelled an RCT, is a secondary analysis of the ROLAIS CRP trial on the same patients; allocation was by the surgeon on the day of surgery and hernia complexity…
  • The extractor could not match 10 numbers to the papers' wording; they are kept and labelled “not verified” in the trials table. [3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 15]
  • DIRECT, labelled an RCT, is a secondary analysis of the ROLAIS CRP trial on the same patients; allocation was by the surgeon on the day of surgery and hernia complexity was classified intraoperatively after allocation [5].
  • ROLAIS had 11 withdrawals before surgery with unbalanced arms (74 robotic vs 65 laparoscopic analysed) and was open-label [4].
  • RIVAL was a pilot with no primary outcome; only 77 of 102 patients completed 2-year follow-up, and the 2020 and 2023 reports describe the same patients [1, 2].
  • ROGER's rTAPP arm had more lateral and larger hernias, and its surgeons were more proficient in TEP, the institutional standard [3].
  • No guideline addressing robotic vs laparoscopic inguinal repair was found, and no included report states its funding or conflicts of interest [9].
  • Coverage: 27 verified numbers (9 pooled) and 16 outcomes not in the draft.
Completeness review12Completeness: 25 gaps found; 1 added, 9 judged not relevant (listed) and 2 notes. Cost is rated Moderate although the answer's own reasoning cites only two trials, setting-specific costs and a non-trial model, which seems inconsistent with the Low overall certainty. Return to activity is rated Very…

Completeness: 25 gaps found; 1 added, 9 judged not relevant (listed) and 2 notes

Notes
  • Cost is rated Moderate although the answer's own reasoning cites only two trials, setting-specific costs and a non-trial model, which seems inconsistent with the Low overall certainty. added on completeness review
  • Return to activity is rated Very low, while the At a Glance and Bottom Line statements describe the results as consistently no benefit, despite the VOLTAIRE signal favouring robotic repair. added on completeness review
Judged not relevant (9)
  • RIVAL wound events/readmissions/VAS/SF-36 at 30 days; neuropathic pain; wound morbidity; QoL at 1-2 years; original RIVAL time/cost; ROLAIS chronic pain/recurrence — Already covered in substance by the answer's pain, QoL, recurrence and complication rows; no numbers given.
  • IL-6 and CRP reductions (ROLAIS) — Inflammatory biomarkers are surrogate outcomes, not asked in the question.
  • DIRECT step-wise times and set-up times — Detail beyond the total operative time already reported.
  • Stray energy camera and working port injury — Histological surrogate; the overall result is already given.
  • Mixed MA POD1 pain SMD and Khoraki cost — Observational-dominated, very low certainty; marginal to the RCT question.
  • R-TAPP vs L-TEP hospital stay and recurrence/complications — Pool likely includes non-randomised studies; the answer already flags it.
  • Da Vinci Xi sensitivity operative time -15.2 min — The answer already notes that the time advantage appears only after removing one study.
  • Return to normal activity 38.5% (pooled review) — Same VOLTAIRE data as 15 (39%) already stated.
  • Median pain day 14; rescue analgesia risk difference; CRP day 3; seroma/hematoma ORs — Minor detail or duplicative of what is already reported.

Full · 31 Oct 2026, 16:17 IST

Edit & re-run

At a glance: Robotic repair has not been shown to improve pain, complications, recurrence or quality of life over laparoscopic repair; it costs more and usually takes longer (low certainty).

  • Pain coughing at 24 h: median NRS 4 with rTAPP vs 5 with TEP, P=0.431 [3]
  • Complications (pooled RCTs): RR 0.76 (95% CI 0.49-1.17), robotic vs laparoscopic [9]
  • Median cost: $3258 with robotic vs $1421 with laparoscopic TAPP, P<.001 [1]
  • Operative time: 75.5 min with robotic vs 40.5 min with laparoscopic (median), P<.001 [1]

Main caveat: a few small trials with experienced surgeons and short follow-up, underpowered for recurrence and chronic pain; one open-label trial (ROLAIS) found fewer complications with robotic repair [4].

Bottom line

Randomised trials show no consistent benefit of robotic over laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair for pain, complications, recurrence, quality of life or return to activity, while robotic repair costs more per case and usually takes longer [1, 2, 3, 6, 9]. The one trial favouring robotic repair (ROLAIS/DIRECT, fewer complications and shorter time) was open-label and single-centre [4, 5]. The trials are underpowered for recurrence and chronic pain, so equivalence on these outcomes cannot be claimed [9].

Certainty: Low Few small, mostly single-centre trials with short follow-up; inconsistent operative-time results; imprecise for rare outcomes.

What this means for clinical practice

Default choice
Laparoscopic (TAPP or TEP) repair; robotic repair offers no proven patient benefit and costs more [1, 3, 9].
Who may benefit
The evidence does not identify any patient group; benefits in obese patients and in recurrent or complex hernias are untested in RCTs, and the only trial favouring robotic repair involved highly experienced robotic surgeons [4, 5].
Counselling
Expect similar pain, recovery, complication and recurrence risk with either approach; robotic surgery usually takes longer and costs more, and long-term data are limited [2, 3, 6].
Cost per case
Robotic repair costs roughly USD 595not traced more (Switzerland, rTAPP $3327 vs TEP $2732) to USD 1837not traced more (US, robotic $3258 vs laparoscopic TAPP $1421) per case [1, 3]; the Italian public-payer model gives an incremental cost of €2,224 [12]; Indian costs are not known.

Conflicting evidence

  • ROLAIS (with its DIRECT secondary analysis, one trial) found fewer complications (23.0% robotic vs 41.5% laparoscopic) and shorter operating time with robotic TAPP [4, 5]. RIVAL and ROGER found no complication difference and longer robotic operating time [1, 3]. The difference may reflect ROLAIS's open-label design, its CRP primary outcome, its unusually high laparoscopic complication rate, unbalanced withdrawals, and very experienced robotic surgeons (at least 100 r-TAPP each) [4, 5].
  • A mostly observational meta-analysis (17 of 18 cohorts observational) reported lower recurrence with robotic repair (RR 0.32, 95% CI 0.17-0.59) [11]. The RCTs show no difference, with only 1 recurrence per arm at 2 years in RIVAL [2, 9]. The observational signal is prone to confounding and is not causal.
  • A meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis found lower pain with robotic TAPP than laparoscopic TEP (MD -1.59, 95% CI -2.41 to -0.76) [13]. Its pool appears to include non-randomised studies, and the finding comes from sensitivity analysis. It conflicts with the blinded ROGER RCT, which compared the same approaches and found no pain difference [3].
  • VOLTAIRE found more robotic patients back to normal activity at 14 days [7, 9]. The blinded Indian RCT found no difference in time to resumption of activities (p=0.180) [6]. VOLTAIRE was small, unequally allocated, used an open-console robot and had ergonomics as its focus [7].
  • Pooled operative-time estimates range from no difference (MD 0.59 min) to clearly longer robotic surgery (MD +30.04 min), with I2 around 98% [10, 11, 14, 15]. The spread is driven by trial design and surgeon experience. The largest pooled estimate (+30.04 min) is mostly observational [11].

Applicability

Case mix
The randomised evidence covers mostly elective, uncomplicated, primary unilateral (some bilateral) inguinal hernias in predominantly male adults, operated on by experienced minimally invasive surgeons [1, 3, 4, 6]. ROGER excluded recurrent hernias [3]. The Indian trial enrolled uncomplicated hernias only [6]. There are no dedicated randomised data for obese patients, recurrent or bilateral hernias, or the robotic learning curve [9]. Most trials compared robotic TAPP with laparoscopic TAPP, but ROGER's comparator was laparoscopic TEP and VOLTAIRE used an open-console robot [3, 7].
India and cost
One blinded single-centre RCT from AIIMS, India found no difference in early pain, rescue analgesia, operative time or return to activity [6]. That trial reported no cost data. All cost figures come from the US, Switzerland and an Italian model, all showing higher robotic cost per case [1, 3, 12]. Indian per-case costs, robot acquisition and maintenance costs, and the cost-effectiveness of robotic repair in Indian hospitals are not known from this evidence. The modelled analyses do not capture robot acquisition or learning-curve effects.
Training
The Italian model suggests confining r-TAPP to training programmes [12]. Surgeon workload findings are mixed: frustration was higher with robotic repair in RIVAL [1], while NASA-TLX workload was lower with rTAPP than TEP in ROGER [3] and ergonomic risk was lower in VOLTAIRE [7]. No RCT has assessed the robotic learning curve. ROGER's authors acknowledge that some rTAPP surgeons may not have completed it [3].

What would change this answer

  • A large multicentre blinded RCT powered for chronic pain and recurrence with at least 2-3 years of follow-up.
  • An independent trial replicating the ROLAIS complication and operative-time advantage with experienced robotic surgeons.
  • RCTs in obese patients and in recurrent or bilateral hernias, and studies of the robotic learning curve.
  • Trial-based cost-effectiveness analyses including robot acquisition and maintenance costs, especially from India or similar health systems.

Challenged by the skeptic

Verdict: the conclusion holds with caveats.

Caveats

  • Randomized evidence is small and low to very low certainty, with about 100-180not verified patients per trial, experienced surgeons and mostly uncomplicated hernias in men. Equivalence cannot be claimed for rare outcomes such as recurrence or chronic pain.
  • RIVAL was an underpowered pilot with no primary outcome and 25% loss to follow-up at 2 years. RIVAL 2020 and 2023 are the same patients.
  • ROLAIS and DIRECT are the same trial and are not independent. ROLAIS reported fewer complications and shorter operative time but was single-centre and open-label.
  • Comparators are heterogeneous: ROGER compared robotic TAPP with laparoscopic TEP, VOLTAIRE used an open-console robot, and the Indian RCT used 2:1 allocation.
  • Operative time results are inconsistent across trials (robotic longer in RIVAL, VOLTAIRE and ROGER, shorter in ROLAIS) with I2 around 98%.
  • Cost evidence is a model-based Italian cost-utility analysis (ICER €44,480/QALY) plus RIVAL cost data ($3258 vs $1421); no RCT-based cost-effectiveness analysis exists, and it ignores robot acquisition and learning-curve effects.
  • The lower-recurrence signal comes from observational data and should not be treated as causal. No guideline addressing robotic vs laparoscopic inguinal repair was found. No RCT data exist on obesity, recurrent or bilateral hernias, or the learning curve.

Not independent

  • RIVAL 2020 and its 1-2 year follow-up report the same 102 patients. [1] [2]
  • DIRECT is a secondary analysis of the ROLAIS trial (138 vs 139 patients), so they are a single trial. [4] [5]
  • The meta-analyses pool the same small set of RCTs and are not independent confirmations. [9] [10] [14] [15] [13]

Picked for extraction (second wave)

  • Robotic TAPP vs laparoscopic TEP meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis; its pain-benefit claim conflicts with the RCTs and its pool composition needs checking. [13]
  • GRADE-assessed RCT-only meta-analysis of r-TAPP vs l-TAPP; the operative-time result depends on removing one study. [14]
  • RCT-only meta-analysis on short-term outcomes; useful for checking trial overlap and the consistency of the pooled operative time. [15]

What the meta-analyses pooled

  • Pooled 18 cohorts and 78,940 participants, mostly observational; the recurrence RR 0.32 is non-randomised. [11]
  • The pool of 6 studies for r-TAPP vs laparoscopic TEP appears to include non-randomised studies, since the abstract recommends further randomized trials. [13]
  • Counts 7 RCTs reported in 9 publications, so the pool includes secondary reports and overlapping trials such as RIVAL follow-up and ROLAIS/DIRECT; the pool also mixes TAPP and TEP comparators. [9]
  • Pools only 3 RCTs; the operative-time advantage emerges only after removing the heterogeneity-driving study (I2 98%). [14]

Evidence against, and guidelines

  • Single-centre open-label RCT found robotic TAPP gave fewer complications, shorter operating time and more same-day discharge, which conflicts with a 'no difference' conclusion — “R-TAPP was associated with a shorter operating time (-13.4 min, P < 0.001), fewer complications (23.0% versus 41.5%, P = 0.029), including fewer haematomas (6.8% versus 18.5%, P = 0.043), and a higher same-day discharge rate (95.9% versus 81.5%, P = 0.012).” [4]
  • Pooled mostly non-randomised data show lower recurrence with robotic repair — “robotic repair was associated with a lower observed recurrence risk (RR 0.32, 95% CI 0.17-0.59; I2 = 0%), although certainty was low and the randomized evidence was imprecise.” [11]
  • Trial sequential analysis suggests lower postoperative pain with robotic TAPP versus laparoscopic TEP — “Sensitivity and trial sequential analyses suggested a significant reduction in postoperative pain with R-TAPP, with TSA confirming robust evidence for lower pain scores” [13]

Other notable findings from this run

  • The extractor could not match 10 numbers to the papers' wording; they are kept and labelled “not verified” in the trials table. [3] [5] [7] [9] [11] [15]
  • DIRECT, labelled an RCT, is a secondary analysis of the ROLAIS CRP trial on the same patients; allocation was by the surgeon on the day of surgery and hernia complexity was classified intraoperatively after allocation [5].
  • ROLAIS had 11 withdrawals before surgery with unbalanced arms (74 robotic vs 65 laparoscopic analysed) and was open-label [4].
  • RIVAL was a pilot with no primary outcome; only 77 of 102 patients completed 2-year follow-up, and the 2020 and 2023 reports describe the same patients [1, 2].
  • ROGER's rTAPP arm had more lateral and larger hernias, and its surgeons were more proficient in TEP, the institutional standard [3].
  • No guideline addressing robotic vs laparoscopic inguinal repair was found, and no included report states its funding or conflicts of interest [9].
